title: CSC3710 2026-08-27: Sets, Cartesian Products, Directed Graphs, Recursive Definitions

questions.q: What is |{a, a, b}|?
questions.explain: Repetitions don't matter in a set, so {a, a, b} = {a, b}, which has 2 elements.

questions.q: Which of these sets are equal to {a, b}?
questions.explain: In a set, neither order nor repetition matters. {{a, b}} has one element (the set {a, b}), and {a, b, ∅} has a third element, ∅.

questions.q: In a multiset, unlike a set, repetitions of elements matter.
questions.explain: Multisets count repetitions. Sets, which this course uses, do not.
2, 3 and 5 are already in ℕ. Adding them again changes nothing, because repetitions don't matter in a set.

questions.q: The power set of a set can be empty.
questions.explain: ∅ is a subset of every set, so ∅ ∈ 𝒫(A) always. A power set has at least one element.

questions.q: What is 𝒫(∅), the power set of the empty set?
questions.explain: The only subset of ∅ is ∅ itself, so 𝒫(∅) = {∅}. That set is not empty. It has one element.

questions.q: What is |𝒫(∅)|?
questions.explain: 𝒫(∅) = {∅}, which contains exactly one element (the empty set).

questions.q: For an arbitrary set A in a universe U, what is |A ∩ Ā|, where Ā is the complement of A?
questions.explain: A and its complement never overlap, so A ∩ Ā = ∅, whose cardinality is 0. This holds no matter what A is.

questions.q: Let A = ∅ in a universe U. Which statement is correct?
choices: Ā = U and A ∩ Ā = U
Ā is undefined when A is empty
questions.explain: The complement of ∅ is everything in the universe, so Ā = U, and ∅ ∩ U = ∅. The cardinality of A ∩ Ā is still 0.

questions.q: To talk about the complement of a set, you need to know the universe you are working in.
questions.explain: Ā is everything in the universe U that is not in A, so it depends on U.

questions.q: What is |{x ∈ ℤ : x² + 5 = 0}|?
questions.explain: x² = −5 has no integer solution (no real one either), so the set is empty.

questions.q: What is |{x ∈ ℝ : x² − 5 = 0}|?
questions.explain: Over the reals the set is {√5, −√5}, so its cardinality is 2. Over the integers it would be empty, because √5 is not an integer.

questions.q: Using the convention in this course, which set is ℕ (the natural numbers)?
questions.explain: In this course 0 is a natural number. The positive naturals {1, 2, 3, ...} get the separate symbol ℕ⁺.

questions.q: Why is writing ℤ = {..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...} considered notation rather than a precise definition?
choices: The "..." depends on the reader recognizing a pattern, and a computer needs a precise recipe for generating the elements
Because the order of elements in ℤ actually matters
Because ℤ is a finite set and should be listed in full
Because negative numbers cannot be elements of a set
questions.explain: The elements are written in order only so that you can see the pattern behind the dots. Someone who doesn't know the pattern, such as a computer, can't interpret "...". Recursive definitions provide the precise recipe that is missing.

questions.q: The set of all numbers that fit in 4 bytes is infinite.
questions.explain: Only finitely many values fit in 4 bytes, so this set is finite and could be listed. The infinite sets are the ones that need a recursive recipe.

questions.q: Let A = {0, 1, 2} and B = {x, y}. What is |A × B|?
Let A = {0, 1, 2} and B = {x, y}. Which of these are elements of B × A?
questions.explain: In B × A the first coordinate comes from B and the second from A. (0, x) and (2, y) belong to A × B instead, and (x, y) has both coordinates from B.

questions.q: For A = {0, 1, 2} and B = {x, y}, A × B = B × A.
questions.explain: Both sets have 6 elements, but the pairs are different. (0, x) ∈ A × B while (x, 0) ∈ B × A, and pairs are ordered.

questions.q: Because order doesn't matter in a set, the pairs (0, x) and (x, 0) are the same.
questions.explain: Order doesn't matter among the elements of a set, but it does matter inside a pair. A pair is a short sequence, like a point in the plane, where (1, 2) ≠ (2, 1).

questions.q: Let B = {x, y} and C = ∅. What is |B × C|?
questions.explain: No pairs can be formed when one side is empty, so B × C = ∅. Equivalently, 2 · 0 = 0.

questions.q: For any two finite sets A and B, which formula gives |A × B|?
questions.explain: Each of the |A| first coordinates pairs with each of the |B| second coordinates, so |A × B| = |A| · |B|.

questions.q: In |A × B| = |A| · |B|, what does the dot mean, and what will a dot between two strings usually mean later in the course?
choices: Multiplication of numbers here, and concatenation for strings
Cartesian product here, and multiplication for strings
Intersection here, and union for strings
questions.explain: Cardinalities are numbers, so · multiplies them. Between strings, · denotes concatenation. Tell which is meant from context.

questions.q: What is a binary relation on a set S?
choices: A subset of S × S × S
questions.explain: "Binary" means two. A binary relation on S is any subset of S × S.

questions.q: A ternary relation on S is a subset of which set?
questions.explain: Ternary means three, so a ternary relation on S is a subset of S × S × S.

questions.q: Let S = {A, B, C, D}. Which of the following are relations on S?
questions.explain: Any subset of S × S is a relation on S, including the empty relation ∅ and S × S itself. {A, B} contains elements, not pairs, and (A, B, C) is a triple.

questions.q: The empty set is a valid relation on any set S.
questions.explain: ∅ is a subset of S × S, so it is a relation: the empty relation. In the phone-number example it means nobody knows anyone's number, not even their own.

questions.q: What does a directed graph consist of?
choices: A set S of nodes and a binary relation R on S
A set S of nodes and a ternary relation on S
Two disjoint sets and a function between them
A set of numbers and the successor function
questions.explain: A directed graph is a set S (the nodes, or vertices) together with a binary relation R on S. Each pair in R is drawn as an arrow.

questions.q: In a directed graph (S, R), the relation R is called the ______ relation. (One word.)
questions.explain: R is the adjacency relation. Node y is adjacent to x when (x, y) ∈ R.

questions.q: In the diagram of a directed graph, how is the pair (x, y) ∈ R drawn?
choices: As an arrow from x to y
As an arrow from y to x
As a line with no direction between x and y
As a single node labeled xy
questions.explain: Each pair (x, y) in the relation becomes an arrow (arc, edge) from x to y.

questions.q: S = {Anne, Ben, Chris, Don}, and (x, y) ∈ R means "x knows y's phone number." How is "Ben knows his own phone number" shown?
choices: The pair (Ben, Ben) in R, drawn as an arrow from Ben back to Ben
It cannot be represented, because a pair needs two different elements
By adding Ben to S a second time
By arrows from Ben to every other node
questions.explain: (Ben, Ben) is a legitimate element of S × S, and it is drawn as a self-loop on Ben.

questions.q: In the "knows the phone number of" graph, if Ben knows Don's number, then Don must also know Ben's number.
questions.explain: Direction matters. (Ben, Don) ∈ R does not imply (Don, Ben) ∈ R, just as pairs are ordered.

questions.q: With S = {Anne, Ben, Chris, Don}, what is the maximum number of arrows a directed graph on S can have, counting self-loops?
questions.explain: The largest relation is S × S itself, with |S| · |S| = 4 · 4 = 16 pairs, including the 4 self-loops.

questions.q: Let S = {1, 2, 3}. How many different binary relations on S are there?
questions.explain: |S × S| = 9, and every subset of S × S is a relation, so there are 2⁹ = 512 relations.

questions.q: A set of ordered pairs and a diagram with arrows can be equivalent representations of the same relation.
questions.explain: The diagram is a picture of the set S and the relation R. This is why machines can be drawn as diagrams but are really sets and relations.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a recursive definition of a set?
questions.explain: Basis (the starting elements), recursive step (rules for building new elements from existing ones), and closure (no other elements).

questions.q: What does the basis of a recursive definition of a set X do?
choices: It designates a finite number of elements as elements of X
It says how to build new elements from old ones
It says that X contains no other elements
It proves that X equals the intended set
questions.explain: The basis lists finitely many starting elements. The recursive step builds new ones, and closure rules out everything else.

questions.q: What does the closure clause of a recursive definition of X say?
choices: X contains only the basis elements and those obtained from them by a finite number of applications of the recursive operations
X is closed under union and intersection
Every element of X must appear in the basis
questions.explain: Closure means "no one else": nothing is in X unless the basis and finitely many applications of the recursive step put it there.

questions.q: The closure clause can be left out of a recursive definition because it is obvious.
questions.explain: Without closure, nothing rules out other elements being in the set, so the definition would be incomplete. Always write it.

questions.q: Recursive definitions of sets matter mainly for which sets?
questions.explain: Finite sets can simply be listed. Recursive definitions give a precise recipe for infinite sets, replacing the vague "...".

questions.q: Which are the three undefined terms in Peano's axioms for the natural numbers?
questions.explain: Peano's axioms define the naturals using three undefined terms: natural (number), zero, and successor.

questions.q: Which is the recursive step in the recursive definition of ℕ that uses the successor function s?
choices: If n ∈ ℕ, then s(n) ∈ ℕ
n ∈ ℕ only if it can be obtained from 0 by finitely many applications of s
If n ∈ ℕ, then n + n ∈ ℕ
questions.explain: "0 ∈ ℕ" is the basis, and the "only if ... finitely many applications" sentence is the closure. The recursive step says the successor of a natural is a natural.

questions.q: In the successor-based definition of ℕ (basis 0, step s), how is the number 3 represented?
questions.explain: Here there is no symbol "3", only zero and its successors: 0, s(0), s(s(0)), s(s(s(0))), ... The third successor of 0 is s(s(s(0))).

questions.q: Peano's original definition of the natural numbers included 0.
questions.explain: Peano's original definition started at 1. The book's version, and this course's, begins with 0.

questions.q: What is the proof technique called that shows a recursively defined set equals an intended set? It is like mathematical induction, but for recursively defined sets.
questions.explain: Structural induction. In practice we instead generate elements, shortest first, and check that they match the target set.

questions.q: λ is the empty string. What is λ · a?
questions.explain: Concatenating with the empty string changes nothing, so λ · a = a.

questions.q: What is the length of the empty string λ?
questions.explain: The empty string contains no symbols, so its length is 0.

questions.q: K is defined by: Basis λ ∈ K. Step: if t ∈ K, then t·a ∈ K and t·b ∈ K. Closure. What new elements does the first application of the recursive step produce?
questions.explain: At first λ is the only element, so t = λ, which gives λ·a = a and λ·b = b.

questions.q: In a recursive step like "if t ∈ K, then t·a ∈ K," t is a placeholder for an element already known to be in K.
questions.explain: t is a variable that stands for some element already in the set. The rule says how to build a new element from it.

questions.q: When generating elements, choosing a t that recreates strings already in the set is an error.
questions.explain: Regenerating an element is harmless, because repetitions don't matter in a set. It just adds nothing new.

questions.q: The empty string λ belongs to the set of even-length strings over {a, b}.
questions.explain: λ has length 0, and 0 is even.

questions.q: Why must λ be in the basis of a recursive definition of the even-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: Concatenation only makes strings longer, so the shortest string λ can never be generated by the recursive step
λ is needed for closure to work
It doesn't have to be. Any even-length string works as the basis
questions.explain: New elements come from concatenation, which never shortens a string. A string that can't be built from anything shorter has to go in the basis.

questions.q: Each option below is a recursive step used with Basis λ ∈ W and a closure clause. Which steps correctly define the set of all even-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: If t ∈ W, then t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb ∈ W
If t ∈ W, then aa·t, ab·t, ba·t, bb·t ∈ W
If t ∈ W, then a·t·a, a·t·b, b·t·a, b·t·b ∈ W
If t ∈ W, then t·a, t·b ∈ W
If t ∈ W, then t·aa, t·bb ∈ W
questions.explain: Appending, prepending, or wrapping with all four 2-symbol combinations generates exactly the even-length strings. t·a and t·b produce odd-length strings such as a, which don't belong. Using only t·aa and t·bb never produces ab or ba.

questions.q: To the even-length definition (Basis λ; Step t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb; Closure), someone adds the rules t·aaaa ∈ W and a·t·aaa ∈ W. What effect does this have?
choices: The definition is still correct. The extra rules are redundant but harmless
The definition is now wrong, because it generates odd-length strings
The definition is now wrong, because a definition may not have redundant rules
The extra rules are needed to generate strings of length 6
questions.explain: Both rules add 4 symbols to an even-length string, so everything they produce is even. Rules 1-4 already generate those strings, so the new rules are redundant. Having more rules than needed is fine. Generating wrong strings is not.

questions.q: Using the rule "if t ∈ W, then a·t·aaa ∈ W" with t = ab, which string is produced?
questions.explain: Put one a in front of t and three a's after it: a · ab · aaa = aabaaa.

questions.q: How many different strings of length 4 are there over the alphabet {a, b}?
questions.explain: There are 4 positions with 2 choices each: 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 = 2⁴ = 16. The four appending rules generate all 16, which shows that extra rules are redundant.

questions.q: Someone defines the even-length strings over {a, b} with Basis aa ∈ W; Step: if t ∈ W, then t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb ∈ W; Closure. What is wrong?
choices: It is incomplete: λ, ab, ba, bb (and every string not starting with aa) are never generated
questions.explain: Every generated string starts with aa, so many even-length strings are missing. The fix is to use the basis λ ∈ W.

questions.q: With Basis λ ∈ X and a closure clause, which recursive step defines {λ, aa, aaaa, aaaaaa, ...}?
choices: If t ∈ X, then t·aa ∈ X
If t ∈ X, then t·a ∈ X
If t ∈ X, then t·aa ∈ X and t·bb ∈ X
If t ∈ X, then t·a ∈ X and t·b ∈ X
questions.explain: Appending aa to an even-length string of a's gives the next one. t·a would produce a, which has odd length, and the rules with b produce strings that aren't in the set.

questions.q: Which recursive definition gives exactly the set of strings over {a, b} that begin with a?
choices: Basis a ∈ Y. Step: if t ∈ Y, then t·a, t·b ∈ Y. Closure
Basis λ ∈ Y. Step: if t ∈ Y, then t·a, t·b ∈ Y. Closure
Basis a ∈ Y. Step: if t ∈ Y, then a·t, b·t ∈ Y. Closure
Basis a ∈ Y. Step: if t ∈ Y, then t·a ∈ Y. Closure
questions.explain: a is the shortest such string, and appending to the end keeps the leading a. Starting from λ produces strings like b. Prepending b produces strings like ba. Appending only a never produces ab.

questions.q: Basis λ ∈ K; Step: if t ∈ K, then t·a, t·b, t·ab ∈ K; Closure. This correctly defines the set of all strings over {a, b}.
questions.explain: t·a and t·b already generate every string. t·ab is redundant (it equals appending a and then b), but it produces only valid strings, so it is harmless.

questions.q: Which of these strings belong to the set of odd-length strings over {a, b}?
questions.explain: a (length 1), bab (length 3), and abbba (length 5) are odd. λ has length 0, which is even, so it is not in this set.

questions.q: What should the basis be in a recursive definition of the odd-length strings Z over {a, b}?
choices: λ ∈ Z, a ∈ Z, and b ∈ Z
questions.explain: a and b are the shortest odd-length strings, and concatenation can't produce them from anything shorter. λ doesn't belong. With only a, strings beginning with b could never be generated if the rules append to the end.

questions.q: For the odd-length strings, a student proposes Basis a, b ∈ Z; Step: if t ∈ Z, then t·a, t·b ∈ Z; Closure. What is wrong?
choices: It generates strings that don't belong, such as aa (even length)
Nothing is wrong. The rules are just redundant
It is missing λ from the basis
questions.explain: Appending one symbol to an odd-length string gives an even-length string. Redundant rules are allowed, but rules that produce strings outside the target set are not.

questions.q: With Basis a, b ∈ Z and a closure clause, which recursive step generates exactly the odd-length strings over {a, b}?
choices: If t ∈ Z, then t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb ∈ Z
If t ∈ Z, then t·a, t·b ∈ Z
If t ∈ Z, then t·a, t·b ∈ Z and t ∈ Z
If t ∈ Z, then t·aaa, t·bbb ∈ Z
questions.explain: To keep the length odd you must add two symbols, not one, and using all four 2-symbol combinations reaches every odd-length string. t·aaa and t·bbb keep the length odd but miss strings such as aab.

questions.q: Using Basis a, b ∈ Z and Step t·aa, t·ab, t·ba, t·bb ∈ Z, how many different strings of length 3 are generated?
questions.explain: From a: aaa, aab, aba, abb. From b: baa, bab, bba, bbb. That is 8 = 2³, which is every string of length 3.

questions.q: A recursive definition may contain redundant rules, as long as every rule produces only strings in the target set and together the rules generate every string in it.
questions.explain: Redundancy is acceptable. It's better to have more rules than not enough. Generating wrong strings, or missing some, is not acceptable.

questions.q: When you list the elements of a set of strings to see its pattern, what order should you use?
questions.explain: Going from the shortest strings to the longest makes the pattern visible, and it shows which short strings must go in the basis. Stop once the pattern is clear.
